analysis.one_liner: Strips California's authority to set its own vehicle emission standards.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended California's authority to set stricter tailpipe pollution rules, never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill repeals the section of the Clean Air Act that lets California get a federal waiver to enforce its own vehicle emission standards, which are stricter than national rules. More than a dozen other states follow California's rules, so repeal would lower standards nationwide. It also ends California-specific cleaner-gasoline rules and state authority over pollution from nonroad engines like construction and farm equipment. The bill never moved past its first committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, automakers and oil refiners would benefit most: they would face one nationwide standard instead of California's stricter rules, which were expected to push faster sales of electric and low-emission vehicles. Vehicle makers could keep selling current engines longer, and fuel producers would no longer have to make special cleaner gasoline for California.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 209(b) of the Clean Air Act, the provision that allows California to obtain a waiver to enforce its own emission standards for new cars and engines.

Ends California-specific exceptions throughout the Clean Air Act, including special fuel rules for waiver states and state authority over nonroad engines, and directs the EPA to terminate any existing waivers within 30 days of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: People living in California and the other states that follow its standards would bear the cost in the form of more tailpipe pollution and a slower shift to cleaner vehicles. California and those state governments would lose authority they have used for over 50 years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Californians and states following its rules

drawbacks.text: Automakers and their allies argue that a patchwork of state standards raises compliance costs and can raise vehicle prices, and that one national standard is simpler; this is the strongest argument for the bill.

Public health and environmental groups counter that stripping California's waiver would allow more air pollution in the most populous state and more than a dozen states that follow its rules, and would slow the transition to cleaner vehicles; the bill includes no replacement standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — uniform national standards that may lower some compliance costs for manufacturers — is small for the public compared with its cost: weaker emission limits in California and a dozen-plus follower states with no federal substitute. It is straightforwardly a deregulation bill whose gains flow to industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its environment subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Doug LaMalfa introduced the bill on September 6, 2022, with Reps. Bost and Ellzey, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
Five Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
The bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change on September 7, 2022, and never received any further action for the rest of the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public in California and the states that follow its emission standards is better off, because the stricter rules stayed on the books. Automakers and refiners did not get the nationwide rollback they would have gained from the bill.

for.name: Doug LaMalfa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal California's Clean Air Act waiver authority.

for.name: Mike Bost and Jake Ellzey
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled any action on the bill; it sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican — the sponsor, two original cosponsors, and five total Republican cosponsors, with no Democratic support — and the Democratic-controlled committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill removes California's special cleaner-gasoline requirements, so refiners would no longer need to produce cleaner-burning fuel for that market; the cost is more air pollution for residents.

Manufacturers would get a single, weaker national standard and could keep selling combustion vehicles longer, though several large automakers had already signed on to California's framework voluntarily and had made investments based on it.
States would lose the Clean Air Act authority they have held for decades to set standards stricter than federal minimums, taking regulatory power away from elected state governments.
